paper_title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multimodal retrieval aims to identify the most relevant images or texts in large collection for given image or text query. Modern systems typically use visionlanguage models (VLMs) to embed different modalities in shared space (Radford et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2025). Retrieval quality depends on these embeddings encoding both which concepts are present and how those concepts are composed. By encoding collection items once and storing their embeddings, this approach can scale to large collections through efficient similarity search (Johnson et al., 2019). In contrast, pairwise models must jointly process the query with each candidate, making them prohibitively expensive at large scale (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019). One important aspect of composition is attributeobject binding: associating each attribute with the correct object (Thrush et al., 2022; Lewis et al., 2024). As illustrated in Figure 1 (top), given query containing golden cannon, tie-dye submarine, and glowing giraffe, model should retrieve candidates preserving these bindings rather than those with the same objects and attributes paired differently. Yet VLM embeddings often behave like bag-of-words matchers, capturing which concepts are present without reliably preserving their bindings (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023). However, existing evidence provides only partial picture of these binding failures, since current benchmarks cover limited range of settings. For example, many benchmarks evaluate only single modality pairing, such as image queries with text candidates (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023), while others use limited attribute vocabulary, often focusing on color (Tang et al., 2023; Burapacheep et al., 2024), and most focus on simple two-object attribute swaps (Dumpala et al., 2024; Koishigarina et al., 2026). This makes it difficult to determine whether these binding failures are general or specific to particular modalities, scene complexity, or attribute types. To study these questions systematically, we introduce SABER (Synthetic Attribute Binding Evaluation for Representations), controlled synthetic benchmark that isolates attributeobject binding by holding the set of objects and attributes fixed while varying their assignments. SABER Figure 2: SABER multiple-choice questions. Each query has four candidates with 210 attribute object pairs: one preserves the bindings, while the others form hard negatives by reassigning attributes. For two-object examples, one negative instead replaces an object or attribute. Although only images are shown, the accompanying captions enable evaluation within and across modalities. Preprint supports unimodal and cross-modal retrieval over images and text, with broad object and attribute vocabularies and scenes containing up to ten objects. We use SABER to evaluate dual-encoder VLMs, such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), as well as newer embedding models derived from multimodal large language models (MLLMs), such as Qwen3-VL-Embedding (Li et al., 2026). Our evaluation on SABER reveals substantial attribute-binding failures across both model families, all four modality pairings, and all levels of scene complexity. We next ask whether these failures can be reduced through targeted binding supervision. Direct multimodal supervision is natural option, but constructing controlled images with the same concepts but different attributeobject assignments is difficult and costly. Text offers simpler alternative: it is cheap to generate, can express visual and non-visual attributes, makes attributeobject bindings explicit rather than implicit in pixels, and enables precisely controlled hard negatives by reassigning attributes among objects. Furthermore, recent studies on MLLMs show that capabilities acquired through text-only supervision can transfer to other modalities (Jiang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). Together, these observations motivate us to ask whether refining pretrained MLLMbased multimodal embedder for specific capability using text alone can transfer improvements across modalities. We test this by finetuning pretrained multimodal embedder exclusively on synthetic attributebinding text (Figure 1, bottom). Despite receiving no image supervision during finetuning, our model achieves the best overall performance on SABER, substantially outperforming all evaluated baselines across all four modality pairings. The gains extend beyond SABER: our model outperforms existing models on all 9 attribute-binding benchmarks tested, spanning natural and synthetic images and diverse text sources, while largely preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Beyond attribute binding, finetuning substantially improves performance on both negation and instance retrieval benchmarks, suggesting that binding-focused supervision can yield broader improvements beyond its original training objective. We will release SABER, our textual finetuning dataset, and our finetuned models to support future research on compositionality and attribute binding.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 MULTIMODAL EMBEDDING MODELS Visionlanguage embedding models have traditionally relied on dual encoders trained contrastively on web-scale imagecaption pairs, as popularized by CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021). Subsequent work has advanced this paradigm through greater scale (Cherti et al., 2023), improved data curation and training recipes (Gadre et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023), and alternative objectives such as SigLIPs sigmoid loss (Zhai et al., 2023). More recently, pretrained MLLMs have been adapted into task-conditioned embedding models for multimodal retrieval. VLM2Vec (Jiang et al., 2025) uses multitask contrastive training to convert pretrained MLLM into an embedding model. LamRA-Ret (Liu et al., 2025) adds language-only retrieval pretraining before finetuning on multimodal retrieval tasks, improving retrieval performance. Qwen3-VL-Embedding (Li et al., 2026) combines large-scale contrastive pretraining with distillation from reranker, which jointly processes each querycandidate pair and assigns it relevance score. The MMEB benchmark series (Jiang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026) evaluates such multimodal embedders across diverse retrieval settings and input modalities. Our work evaluates attributeobject binding in both CLIP-style dual encoders and MLLM-based embedders. 2.2 COMPOSITIONALITY IN VISIONLANGUAGE REPRESENTATIONS Prior work has repeatedly found that VLM embeddings exhibit bag-of-words behavior, with limited sensitivity to compositional structure. Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022) illustrates this using captions containing the same words but expressing different compositions, such as some plants surrounding lightbulb and lightbulb surrounding some plants, which models often struggle to match to the correct images. ARO (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023) and SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023) probe these failures more systematically using hard negatives that swap or replace objects and attributes, modify relations, or alter word order. Preprint Multiple explanations for this bag-of-words behavior have motivated different mitigation strategies. One line of work attributes these failures to insufficient compositional signal or other biases in standard imagetext training data (Doveh et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2024; Gurung et al., 2025). Accordingly, proposed remedies include augmenting the training data with compositional hard negatives (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024) and improving the caption density and imagetext alignment (Doveh et al., 2023). However, beyond being costly, automatically constructed multimodal supervision can also be noisy, with artifacts in text perturbations, hallucinations in generated captions, and unintended variation in synthetic images. second explanation is that single global embedding may be too blunt representation for compositional structure, requiring it to encode diverse information, such as content, appearance, spatial layout, and attributeobject bindings, all within the same vector (Kamath et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025; Weller et al., 2026). Methods addressing this bottleneck either retain token and patch representations for late-interaction scoring (Kang et al., 2025; Assouel et al., 2025) or use pairwise scorers to directly model interactions between inputs (Krojer et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024a;b). We instead use synthetic text-only supervision, where attributeobject bindings can be manipulated precisely and at scale to construct controlled hard negatives, without requiring controlled image generation or changing the standard single-vector architecture and inference procedure. 2.3 ATTRIBUTE-BINDING BENCHMARKS Existing attribute-binding benchmarks vary considerably in scope and design. VG-Attribution (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023) and SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023) use natural images but are limited to imagetext retrieval. SugarCrepe++ (Dumpala et al., 2024) extends SugarCrepe with texttext retrieval, while ColorSwap (Burapacheep et al., 2024) and BiVLC-Swap-Att. (Miranda et al., 2024) leverage synthetic images to enable bidirectional imagetext retrieval. More controlled benchmarks isolate attributeobject binding through explicitly constructed scenes with limited vocabularies. NCD (Tang et al., 2023; Anwar et al., 2025) evaluates color binding in scenes containing fruits and vegetables. CLEVR-based benchmarks (Johnson et al., 2017; Koishigarina et al., 2026) use rendered geometric objects and scale to scenes with up to ten bindings, while PUG:SPAR (Bordes et al., 2023) and PUG:SPARE (Koishigarina et al., 2026) systematically vary attributes in rendered animal scenes. Despite this greater control, evaluation remains limited to imagetext retrieval. Figure 9 in the Appendix provides representative examples from each benchmark. sections.title: 3 SABER BENCHMARK
sections.content: Existing attribute-binding benchmarks are limited in modality coverage, vocabulary, or the number of bindings per sample, and rely on small candidate-set evaluations without assessing large-gallery retrieval with multiple valid positives (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Burapacheep 4 Preprint Figure 3: Nested SABER chains. Nine linked MCQs form chain from two to ten objects, read left to right and top to bottom. Each successive query adds one binding while preserving all earlier ones. Half of SABERs MCQs are organized into such chains, allowing later correct candidates to serve as additional positives for earlier queries in large-gallery retrieval. et al., 2024; Miranda et al., 2024; Koishigarina et al., 2026). As result, they provide only partial view of how well current representations preserve attributeobject bindings. To address these limitations, we introduce SABER (Synthetic Attribute Binding Evaluation for Representations), benchmark structured as 4-way multiple-choice questions (MCQs), whose candidates can also be pooled for large-gallery retrieval. SABER covers all four image and text modality pairings, draws from sets of 232 everyday objects and 50 visual attributes spanning colors, materials, patterns, and effects, and scales to scenes with up to ten objects. Table 1 summarizes the differences between SABER and prior benchmarks. Each of our MCQs, illustrated in Figures 1 and 2, contains query and four candidates, each represented by both an image and caption. One candidate preserves the querys attributeobject bindings, while the remaining three are hard negatives that alter these assignments. Except for one negative in the two-object setting (Candidate 1 in Figure 2), all candidates contain the same objects and attributes as the query, isolating binding from other challenges such as object recognition. The benchmark draws from our sets of 232 everyday objects and 50 visual attributes. Sampled objects and attributes are paired in templated query caption, such as sandy snowboard and pink cherry. This fixed phrasing minimizes linguistic variation unrelated to attributeobject binding. After constructing the corresponding candidate captions, we synthesize the query and candidate images using GPT Image 2 (OpenAI, 2026), with instructions specifying neutral CLEVR-style scenes and consistent realizations of each attribute across all five images in an MCQ. This keeps attribute appearance consistent across candidates, so that their visual differences primarily reflect changes in binding. All generated images are manually inspected to ensure that the intended objects and attribute bindings are rendered correctly, yielding unambiguous MCQs with unique correct answer. SABER contains 200 MCQs for each scene size from 2 to 10 objects: 100 independent examples and 100 arranged into nested chains, as illustrated in Figure 3. Each successive query in chain adds one attributeobject binding while preserving earlier ones. Overall, this yields 1,800 queries and 7,200 candidates, or 9,000 imagecaption pairs. We evaluate models on SABER using two complementary protocols: 4-way MCQ and large-gallery retrieval. In the MCQ setting, the model ranks four candidates by similarity to the query and succeeds when the binding-preserving candidate ranks first. In the retrieval setting, each query is ranked against all 7,200 candidates, with any candidate containing all query bindings treated as positive. Independent queries have one positive, while nested-chain queries may have multiple positives from 5 Preprint later scenes that preserve earlier bindings. This reflects practical retrieval, where the queried bindings may appear within larger, more complex scene. Further benchmark-generation details appear in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4 TEXT-ONLY FINETUNING FOR ATTRIBUTE BINDING
sections.content: To assess the binding capabilities of current embedding models, we evaluate range of CLIP-style dual encoders (Radford et al., 2021; Bolya et al., 2025), including compositional and attributebinding variants such as TripletCLIP (Patel et al., 2024), READ-CLIP (Kwon et al., 2025), and LABCLIP (Koishigarina et al., 2026) together with recent MLLM-based embedders (Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Table 2 reveals clear binding failures across existing models on SABER, motivating targeted finetuning to improve binding sensitivity. We therefore turn to text-only finetuning on synthetic attribute-binding data. Text is particularly well suited to this setting because bindings are explicit and easy to manipulate, enabling precisely controlled hard negatives without the incidental variation that can arise in generated images. Using Gemma 4 (Google DeepMind, 2026), we construct 200,000 finetuning triplets, each containing query, positive, and hard negative. Each query specifies two or three attributeobject pairs, with the positive then contextualizing those bindings. For example, the query red banner and torn flag may be paired with High above the roar of the crowd, . . . there waved red banner and torn flag. We construct hard negative by permuting either the attributes or the objects, so that it differs from the positive only in its attributeobject assignments. To reduce shortcut cues, we choose attributes that remain plausible for all objects in each example and randomize the order of the attributeobject pairs between the query and the positive. Although the finetuning triplets are entirely textual, our goal is to improve attribute binding across all text and image modality pairings. More formally, let xm denote query expressing set of attribute object bindings in modality {Text, Image}, and let xn denote binding-preserving positive and binding-conflicting negative, respectively, in modality {Text, Image}. Ideally, the embedding model should place the positive closer to the query under every modality pairing: ), fθ(xn where fθ is the multimodal embedder and is cosine similarity in the shared embedding space. Given textual query tq, positive t+, and hard negative t, we minimize the following triplet loss (Schroff et al., 2015) Ltext = [D(fθ(tq), fθ(t)) D(fθ(tq), fθ(t+)) + γ]+ , where γ is the triplet margin and [z]+ = max(z, 0) denotes the positive-part function. Unlike CLIP-style dual encoders with separate image and text encoders, MLLMs contain parameters that are shared across modalities. Although we optimize only the textual loss above, updating these shared parameters from textual triplets also affects the representations produced for images, providing mechanism for the learned binding behavior to transfer to the other modality. We finetune Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B (Li et al., 2026) with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) using this objective and subsequently apply LiNeS (Wang et al., 2025) to rescale the layer-wise parameter updates and mitigate forgetting of pretrained capabilities. Appendix provides additional details on the finetuning dataset and optimization procedure. Appendix ablates the finetuning data and LiNeS and analyzes attention changes before and after finetuning. Appendix shows that our finetuning recipe extends to other MLLM backbones. Appendix compares finetuning with text versus images on SABER and shows that textual supervision yields stronger cross-modal retrieval performance.

sections.title: 6 FROM ATTRIBUTE BINDING TO NEGATION
sections.content: Attribute binding is only one form of compositional sensitivity. To assess whether binding-focused finetuning improves compositional sensitivity more broadly, we evaluate our models on NegBench (Alhamoud et al., 2025), which tests negation understanding. We compare the base Qwen3VL-Embedding-8B, our finetuned model, and variant trained after removing the 7.1% of finetuning examples containing negation terms such as no, without, and neither. This ablation tests whether 1MMEB-v3 reports 24 VisDoc tasks but enumerates 27; we score all 27 for every model. 8 Preprint gains arise from incidental exposure to negation rather than transfer from binding supervision. We also include Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B, stronger pairwise model, as an additional reference. NegBench groups MCQs according to the type of the correct statement: affirmation describes present objects, negation absent objects, and hybrid both. Each MCQ contains the correct answer together with one additional candidate of each type. Table 5 shows that finetuning improves overall accuracy by 9.3 points on the COCO (Lin et al., 2014) subset and 10.5 points on the PASCAL VOC 2007 (Everingham et al., 2010) subset, driven mainly by large gains on hybrid cases. In these cases, the model must distinguish candidates such as bowl but no cup and cup but no bowl, which share the same bag of words but assign negation to different objects. This closely resembles our attribute-binding setup, where correctness depends on associating the correct property with each object. By contrast, in the affirmation and negation groups, the two same-type candidates contain different bags of words. Notably, the negation-filtered variant retains nearly all of these gains, suggesting transfer from binding supervision rather than direct negation exposure. sections.title: 7 BROADER BENEFITS: INSTANCE-LEVEL RETRIEVAL
sections.content: We next ask whether binding-focused finetuning benefits instance retrieval, where the goal is to retrieve the same object instance rather than its category. Instances are often distinguished by their attributes, such as the color of shirt, suggesting that improved binding could strengthen instancelevel representations. We therefore evaluate Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B and our finetuned model on ILIAS (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025), INSTRE (Wang & Jiang, 2015), PODS (Sundaram et al., 2025), Paris6K (Philbin et al., 2008), Oxford5K (Philbin et al., 2007), and Sculptures6K (Arandjelovic & Zisserman, 2011), covering eight imageimage settings and one textimage setting. Table 6 reports mAP across all settings. Our finetuned model improves over the pretrained model in every setting, with gains ranging from +2.1 to +9.9 mAP. To examine whether these gains reflect better discrimination among visually similar instances, we evaluate retrieval separately within ILIASs fine-grained object categories, such as cakes or cards. Within each category, each image is used in turn as query against the remaining images, with images depicting the same instance treated as relevant. Our model improves over the pretrained model in all 38 fine-grained categories, with mean mAP increase of 8.5 points. sections.title: 8 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Our results reveal gap between broad retrieval capability and precise attributeobject binding. We introduce SABER to characterize these failures and show that targeted text-only finetuning improves 9 Preprint binding across modality pairings, and that these gains transfer to independent benchmarks, negation, and instance retrieval, while largely preserving general multimodal performance. In Appendix G, we show these gains extend beyond attribute swaps to partial-description formulation. Appendix shows that supplying the embedding model with binding-specific instructions helps but does not match the gains from our finetuning. key limitation is that SABER is synthetic, and generated images may contain unintended variation in appearance, layout, object size, or orientation beyond the intended binding changes. Taken together, our findings suggest that compositional precision is distinct dimension of embedding quality that warrants explicit evaluation and optimization. AI USE STATEMENT Generative AI tools were used for data generation and in several experimental components of this work. Gemma 4 was used to generate synthetic text examples for our finetuning dataset, while GPTImage-2 was used to generate the synthetic SABER images from author-defined object and attribute sets. Multiple visionlanguage models were also used to propose and refine candidate instructions for the instruction-sensitivity experiment; the authors reviewed and edited these instructions, selected the final set, and conducted all evaluations. Generative AI tools were additionally used to support code implementation, figure design, and the drafting and editing of portions of the manuscript. AI tools were also used to assist with literature search and the identification of related work; all referenced works were independently verified and read by the authors. All AI-assisted code, figures, experimental materials, and manuscript text were reviewed and approved by the authors. These tools did not independently formulate the research questions, design the methodology, interpret the results, or determine the conclusions. The authors take full responsibility for all aspects of this work. ETHICS STATEMENT This work does not involve the collection of new human-subject data and uses only existing research benchmarks and synthetically generated data. Some third-party benchmarks contain publicly sourced images, but we do not use identity information or analyze personal attributes. Attributebinding performance should not be interpreted as evidence of broader fairness, safety, or suitability for deployment. Our results may inherit biases and limitations from the pretrained embedding models, generative models, and datasets used in this work. Licenses and applicable usage terms for third-party datasets and models are reported in Table 20 in the Appendix. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We provide detailed descriptions of the SABER benchmark construction, textual finetuning data generation, training procedure, and evaluation protocols in the main paper and appendices. We will release SABER, our textual finetuning dataset, and the weights of our finetuned models to facilitate reproducibility and support future research on compositionality and attribute binding. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS We thank Stephanie Fu for helpful discussions throughout the project, and Narek Tumanyan for providing valuable comments on earlier versions of the paper.

sections.title: A SABER BENCHMARK DETAILS
sections.content: This section provides additional details on SABERs attribute sets, candidate construction, textual realization, image synthesis, and benchmark subsets. A.1 BUILDING BLOCKS The benchmark is generated from two lists: set of 232 everyday objects (e.g., toothbrush, teapot, kayak) and set of 50 visual attributes (e.g., red, glowing, sandy). The attributes are grouped into 6 semantic categories, summarized in Table 7. In addition to semantic category, each attribute is assigned type that determines how it is realized during generation: standalone (27): fixed appearance with no free slot, such as camouflage or transparent. Some attributes use fixed generation form; for example, soap-bubble is expressed as iridescent soap-bubble. single-color (4): template with one color slot, e.g., glowing {color} glowing. two-color (6): template with two distinct color slots, e.g., striped {color1} and {color2} striped. fixed-variant (13): template instantiated from small closed set of variants, e.g., wooden {light-brown, dark-brown} wooden. Color slots are filled from palette of nine basic colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, pink, white, and black. For two-color attributes, the two sampled colors are always distinct. Table 7: Number of SABER attributes in each semantic category. Attribute category Basic color Other color Metallic Material Pattern Effect Total # 9 2 3 19 15 2 50 A.2 EXAMPLE STRUCTURE To construct multiple-choice question (MCQ) consisting of one query and four candidate answers, each with attributeobject bindings, we sample distinct objects and distinct attributes and pair them to form the query. We then derive four candidates, according to the following rules: candidate 1 (binding-preserving): preserves the query bindings while reordering the attributeobject pairs. candidate 2 (attribute-swap): keeps the objects in the same order as candidate 1 but permutes the attributes across them, producing incorrect attributeobject bindings. candidate 3 (object-swap): keeps the attributes in the same order as candidate 1 but permutes the objects across them, producing another incorrect binding assignment. candidate 4 (joint-swap): permutes both the objects and the attributes, producing another incorrect binding assignment. For 3, the four candidates are required to have pairwise distinct binding assignments; any permutation that duplicates an existing candidate is rejected and resampled. For = 2, where only two one-to-one assignments are possible, candidate 4 instead preserves one query binding and replaces either the object or the attribute in the other binding with new element not present in the query. For visualization purposes, the candidates are shown in shuffled order in Figures 1 and 2 of the main paper. 15 Preprint A.3 DUAL TEXTUAL REALIZATION Each query and candidate is expressed as conjunction of its attributeobject pairs, such as striped cube and transparent kite. Indefinite articles (a/an) are selected automatically based on pronunciation. For each query and candidate, we produce two parallel textual forms: the text form, which uses the basic attribute forms (e.g., striped cube) and constitutes the benchmarks text modality; the generation form, which uses the fully instantiated appearance (e.g., white and orange striped cube) and is used to construct the text-to-image prompt. Within each example, every attribute is instantiated once and reused across the query and all candidates. For instance, if striped is realized as white and orange striped, that same realization is used wherever striped appears. This keeps each attribute visually consistent across all images and reduces appearance variation unrelated to binding. A.4 IMAGE SYNTHESIS Images are synthesized from the generation-form captions of the query and each candidate using GPT-Image-2 at 1024 1024 resolution and medium quality. The rendering prompt requests CLEVR-style 3D scene on neutral gray background in which the listed objects are clearly separated and scattered rather than laid out in row, with each object appearing exactly once. central requirement of the prompt is binding locality: every attribute must apply only to its assigned object. In particular, the prompt specifies that colors, materials, patterns, textures, and visual effects must not transfer, blend, or bleed across objects. To reduce positional shortcuts, each rendered image is horizontally flipped with probability 0.5. Finally, all generated images are manually screened to verify that the depicted attributeobject bindings match their associated captions. A.5 BENCHMARK SUBSETS For each object count {2, . . . , 10}, SABER contains 200 MCQ examples, evenly split between independently sampled examples and nested chains. The independently sampled examples provide broader coverage of object, attribute, and binding combinations. In contrast, each nested chain starts with two-object example and adds one new attributeobject binding at each subsequent object count, while reshuffling the order of the pairs. Thus, later queries preserve all bindings from earlier queries while introducing additional objects. Their binding-preserving candidates therefore serve as additional positives for earlier queries in large-gallery retrieval. TEXT-ONLY FINETUNING FOR ATTRIBUTE BINDING This section provides additional details on the construction of our text-only finetuning dataset, including its seven construction types, diversity controls, and validation procedure, as well as the training split, optimization setup, and evaluation of generalization to held-out binding structures. B.1 GENERATION SETUP We generate the finetuning dataset using Gemma 4 31B-IT (Google DeepMind, 2026). For each example, the model selects the objects and attributes and writes contextualized positive caption expressing the intended attributeobject bindings. From this structured output, we construct the query and two hard negatives. The query lists the attributeobject pairs in randomized order, while the negatives are formed by permuting either the attributes or the objects in the positive caption. This short-query, longer-candidate format reflects practical retrieval, where concise search query is matched against gallery of items that may contain the queried content alongside additional information. Thus, the positive and both negatives contain exactly the same words and differ only in their attributeobject bindings. Each example is then automatically validated, with failures discarded and regenerated. The final dataset contains 100,000 examples distributed across the seven construction types shown in Table 8. 16 Preprint Table 8: Number of finetuning examples by construction type. Construction type pair swap attr bundle predicative triple bind cycle triple bind swap deferred bind anaphoric deferred bind respective Total # 20,000 20,000 20,000 10,048 9,952 9,417 10,583 100,000 B.2 CONSTRUCTION TYPES Each example belongs to one of seven construction types, which vary the number of attributeobject pairs and the sentence structure that expresses their bindings. Table 9 shows one example of each type: pair swap: two objects, each directly preceded by its attribute. The attribute negative exchanges the two attributes, and the object negative exchanges the two nouns. triple bind cycle: three objects. The attribute negative rotates the three attributes by one position, and the object negative does the same with the nouns, so all three bindings are wrong in each negative. triple bind swap: three objects, but only two pairs are transposed. One of the three pairs, chosen at random, remains correctly bound in both negatives, so the model must locate which bindings changed rather than simply detect that something changed. attr bundle: two objects, each carrying two attributes from different semantic slots (e.g., color and material, or age and condition), which prevents redundant pairs such as red crimson. The attribute negative exchanges the attributes of only one slot, so it differs from the positive by single word per object; the object negative exchanges the nouns. predicative: two objects whose attributes are detached from their nouns through copula, change-of-state verb, or relative clause (e.g., the book was dated). The adjacent phrase attribute object may not appear anywhere in the caption. deferred bind anaphoric: both nouns are introduced before either attribute appears, and the attributes are then assigned by back-reference (e.g., the former . . . the latter or the first . . . the second). In half of the examples the second object is described first, so the reference must actually be resolved. Ambiguous references such as bare it or they are rejected. deferred bind respective: both nouns are introduced before either attribute appears, and the attributes are then assigned jointly in noun order (e.g., . . . were new and neat respectively), so the binding is carried entirely by word order. In the predicative and deferred bind types, attributes are not adjacent to their objects, so the correct bindings must be recovered from sentence structure rather than local word co-occurrence. B.3 DIVERSITY CONTROLS Repeatedly sampling language model without additional constraints tends to produce narrow range of vocabulary, styles, and sentence structures. To increase diversity, we therefore sample several properties independently for each example and specify them in the prompt: Context. Each prompt samples from 1,000 seed scenes, with optional time-of-day and weather modifiers, yielding 81,000 distinct contexts. It additionally samples from 32 writing registers (e.g., news caption, field notebook, auction listing, maintenance log) and 16 sentence-opener styles. Each example is assigned one of four target length bands (1015, 1622, 23 30, or 3142 words), shifted upward by 24 words for the three-object constructions. The target length band is chosen so that it is long enough to accommodate the assigned bindingdistance range; the deferred bind constructions therefore use only the three longer bands. The target band is specified in the prompt and enforced during validation, allowing one word below and four words above the band. Binding distance. Each example is assigned target range for the distance over which an attributeobject binding must be resolved, preventing the relevant words from always appearing close together. For constructions in which attributes directly precede their objects, this is the minimum number of words separating consecutive core phrases (windows from 02 up to 1426 words for two objects, and up to 713 for three, where the minimum is taken over both gaps); for predicative, it is the smaller of the two distances between 18 Preprint an object and its attribute; and for deferred bind, it is the span from the final object mention to the first attribute assignment. The target range is specified in the prompt and enforced during validation. Distractors. For pair swap, predicative, and the two deferred bind construction types, the prompt asks for up to three additional attributeobject pairs that are woven into the sentence but do not appear in the query. The positive text therefore describes more than the query asks about, so the model must locate the queried bindings among unrelated ones rather than treat every attributeobject pair in the text as relevant. Vocabulary. Examples that duplicate the complete set of attributes and objects from an earlier example of the same construction type are rejected. To prevent small set of words from dominating the dataset, each attribute and object is subject to running frequency cap over the examples accepted so far. The cap is the larger of ten occurrences and fixed fraction of accepted examples, with the fraction scaled by the number of attributes per example: 1.5%, 2.25%, and 3% for constructions with two, three, and four attributes, respectively. This keeps the allowance per attribute slot constant while preventing frequent words from becoming overrepresented early in generation. Each prompt also includes an avoid list containing the 100 most recently used and 40 most frequent words, together with hard ban list for words that have already reached the cap. Attribute pool. Frequency caps alone were insufficient to diversify the attributes, because the model continued to favor small set of common adjectives even after they had reached the cap, causing many generated examples to be rejected. We therefore also provide attribute suggestions in the prompt. These are drawn from curated pool of 772 common adjectives organized into 19 families that apply broadly across object classes, including color, texture, material, condition, size, age, and value. The prompt includes the least-used attributes from each family that have not yet reached the frequency cap, sampled per family so that no single family dominates the suggestions. The pool serves only as source of suggestions: attributes outside the pool are also accepted if they pass validation. B.4 VALIDATION Each generated example passes structural validation step before being added to the dataset; failures are discarded, logged, and regenerated. In addition to the length, binding-distance, and vocabulary constraints described in Section B.3, validation checks that the example has the intended binding structure. Attributes are required to be single words, and all objects and attributes must be distinct, each appearing exactly once in the query, positive, and both negatives, so that all queried bindings are specified unambiguously. Each negative must be word-level permutation of the positive (treating and an as equivalent) that breaks every queried binding, introduces all intended incorrect bindings, and remains distinct from both the positive and the other negative. Article-agreement errors created by permutation (e.g., envelope) are repaired automatically, and any remaining article error not already present in the positive causes the example to be rejected. Finally, validation enforces the structural constraints of each construction: attributes directly precede their objects in pair swap, triple bind, and attr bundle; are never adjacent to their objects in predicative; and in deferred bind are never adjacent to their objects and appear only after both objects have been introduced. B.5 FINETUNING AND EVALUATION We hold out both deferred bind construction types entirely and randomly split the remaining 80,000 examples into training, validation, and test sets in an 80/10/10 ratio, yielding 64,000, 8,000, and 8,000 examples, respectively. Each example yields two triplets, one per hard negative, for total of 200,000 triplets: 128,000 for training, 16,000 for validation, 16,000 for testing, and 40,000 heldout deferred bind triplets. Each model is finetuned using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters with rank r=4, α=4, and zero dropout, applied to the query, key, value, and output projections in every decoder layer. The vision Preprint tower remains frozen, resulting in 3.8M trainable parameters for the 8B model. All inputs use the models default instruction. Training runs for one epoch on single B200 GPU using AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019), with constant learning rate of 5105 and weight decay 0.01. The objective is hinge triplet loss over cosine similarity with margin γ=0.05. After training, we apply LiNeS (Wang et al., 2025) post hoc to rescale the LoRA updates across decoder layers using the default setting of Wang et al. (2025). We evaluate attribute-binding performance using triplet accuracy, defined as the fraction of triplets for which the positive is closer to the query than the negative; chance performance is 50%. Table 10 reports this metric across all evaluated models on the in-distribution test set and the two held-out deferred bind constructions, which test generalization to binding structures never seen during training. sections.title: D GENERALIZATION ACROSS MULTIMODAL EMBEDDERS
sections.content: To test whether our finetuning strategy is specific to Qwen3-VL-Embedding or generalizes to other multimodal embedders, we apply the same recipe to two additional model families, UEmbed (Song et al., 2026) and WeMM-Embedding (Zhou et al., 2026), each at 2B and 9B parameters. Both are built on Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026), whose hybrid decoder uses softmax attention only every fourth layer, with linear-attention blocks in the remaining layers. We retain the training setup from our main experiments, using the same data, learning rate, and LiNeS. We apply rank-4 LoRA to the query, key, value, and output projections of the full-attention layers and evaluate the checkpoint after one epoch. Each model uses its official prompting and pooling scheme; for UEmbed, we use the dense embedding rather than its sparse representation. The unmodified public checkpoint serves as the baseline for comparison with its finetuned counterpart on SABER and MMEB-v3. As shown in Table 14, binding-focused finetuning consistently improves SABER across both model families, model sizes, and all four modality pairings. The largest gains generally occur in texttext retrieval: UEmbed improves by 48.6 and 44.3 points at 2B and 9B, respectively, while WeMMEmbedding improves by 37.5 and 31.9 points. Importantly, these gains transfer beyond the text modality used for training. All four models also improve on both cross-modal settings and on imageimage retrieval, with particularly large cross-modal gains for the 9B models. For example, WeMM-Embedding-9B improves from 30.6 to 58.7 in textimage retrieval and from 32.6 to 64.4 in imagetext retrieval. This consistent transfer suggests that the effect is not specific to the Qwen3-VL-Embedding backbone and that text-only binding supervision can improve multimodal representations across different embedding architectures. sections.title: E COMPARING TEXT AND IMAGE FINETUNING FOR ATTRIBUTE BINDING
sections.content: Our main approach uses text-only supervision because text makes attributeobject bindings explicit and easy to manipulate, enabling precisely controlled hard negatives. However, this high degree of control may also make text supervision artificially clean. Images inevitably introduce variation in appearance, pose, lighting, size, spatial arrangement, and other visual factors. Although such variation makes the learning problem harder, it may also provide useful regularization, forcing the model to learn binding representations that are robust to nuisance variation rather than relying on the clean structure of text. We therefore ask whether text or image supervision is more effective for learning attribute binding. To study this, we split SABER into 70/10/20 train/validation/test split and finetune on increasing amounts of either text or image supervision, corresponding to 10%, 20%, 35%, and 70% of the full benchmark. sections.title: F EVALUATION AND ANALYSIS ON INSTANCE RETRIEVAL
sections.content: F.1 DATASETS AND EVALUATION PROTOCOLS We evaluate on six instance-retrieval benchmarks spanning landmarks, sculptures, household objects, and diverse object instances. Oxford5K (Philbin et al., 2007) and Paris6K (Philbin et al., Images labeled good or ok are 2008) evaluate landmark retrieval using cropped query regions. treated as relevant, while junk images are ignored during evaluation. Sculptures6K (Arandjelovic & Zisserman, 2011) similarly uses cropped queries, with benchmark-specific relevance annotations. PODS (Sundaram et al., 2025) contains household objects photographed under several distribution shifts and evaluates retrieval across reference views of each object. ILIAS (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025) contains diverse object instances and supports both imageimage and textimage retrieval over shared image database. INSTRE (Wang & Jiang, 2015) contains single-object images (INSTRE-S) and images depicting pairs of objects (INSTRE-M). Following the original protocol, we evaluate queries from INSTRE-S against INSTRE-S, and queries from INSTRE-M against either INSTRE-S or the combined INSTRE-S+M gallery. In the combined setting, relevance depends on whether retrieved image contains one or both query instances, with images containing both receiving higher relevance. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B and our finetuned model under identical conditions on each benchmark, following the benchmark-specific protocols described above. Images are embedded in full unless benchmark provides ground-truth query crop, in which case we use the specified crop. We do not include auxiliary distractor sets. Accordingly, comparisons between the pretrained and finetuned models are directly controlled, while absolute performance may differ from published results that use additional distractors. Quantitative results across all benchmarks and evaluation settings are reported in Table 6 of the main paper. Figure 5 complements these results with qualitative imageimage retrieval examples on ILIAS. We show queries for which either the pretrained or finetuned model has large relative advantage, together with their top-5 retrieved images. Across all 1,232 ILIAS image queries, the finetuned model performs better on 923, the pretrained model on 108, and the two models tie on 201. We consider its 38 named fine-grained classes, spanning 491 object instances across seven top-level categories. sections.title: G ATTRIBUTE BINDING BEYOND ATTRIBUTE SWAPS
sections.content: SABER follows common MCQ setup in which queries and candidates contain the same objects and attributes, with the correct candidate preserving the querys bindings and incorrect candidates reassigning attributes across objects (Yuksekgonul et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Bordes et al., 2023). We next ask whether the resulting gains reflect broader improvements in attribute binding or specialization to this swap-based setting. We adopt complementary formulation from prior work (Lewis et al., 2024) in which candidates describe only part of the query. Given an image containing two attributed objects, the model retrieves text naming single attributeobject pair; the correct candidate preserves one of the images bindings, whereas the hard negative candidates pair each object with the other objects attribute. Because 27 Preprint both concepts in each candidate appear in the image, concept presence alone cannot distinguish the correct binding, and learned concept associations can even favor the mismatch (Tang et al., 2023). We evaluate this formulation on the full CLEVR-based imagetext benchmark introduced by Lewis et al. (2024), combining all of its splits into single benchmark that we denote CLEVR-bind. Since CLEVR-bind uses only two-object scenes, Figure 7 compares model performance on CLEVRbind with SABER in the corresponding two-object imagetext setting. Across the ten evaluated models, the scores are positively correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.89; Kendall τ = 0.78). Our finetuned 8B model improves over its pretrained counterpart and achieves the highest accuracy in both settings. Together, these results suggest that its gains extend beyond attribute swaps to this partial-description formulation. Figure 7: Agreement across attribute-binding formulations. CAN BINDING-SPECIFIC INSTRUCTIONS REPLACE FINETUNING? Qwen3-VL-Embedding conditions its embeddings on task instruction, and its developers recommend tailoring these instructions to the target task to improve performance (Li et al., 2026). This raises the question of whether attribute binding can be improved through instruction choice alone, without modifying the model weights. We evaluate the default instruction (Represent the users input.) alongside 40 binding-specific alternatives on SABER and the MMEB-v3 image tasks, using both the pretrained and finetuned 8B models. Figure 8 shows the resulting trade-off between SABER and MMEB-v3 performance across instruction choices. For the pretrained Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B model, binding-specific instructions improve SABER accuracy at the expense of MMEB-v3 image performance, revealing trade-off between the two. Although our model is finetuned only with the default instruction, it remains instruction-sensitive and exhibits similar trade-off under the same alternatives. Crucially, with the default instruction alone, our finetuned model already surpasses the highest SABER accuracy achieved by the pretrained model under any of the 40 binding-specific instructions.
